To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
glutathione regulates ascorbic acid metabolism in rat hepatoma and hepatocytes by controlling the expression of ascorbic-acid transporters.

the intracellular redox state of hepatocytes controls the expression of the transporters that mediate the uptake of ascorbic and dehydroascorbic acids, thereby determining the availability of these vitamin C species to the cells.
glutathione regulates ascorbate transport in rat hepatoma cells by controlling the expression and sub-cellular localization of the ascorbate transporters SVCT-1 and SVCT-2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel mechanisms regulating vitamin C transport and metabolism.
the regulation of ascorbic-acid transport by the cellular redox environment.
the regulation of vitamin C transporters in hepatocytes and hepatocarcinoma cells by glutathione and the consequences of these effects on the intracellular ascorbic acid content.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

glutathione is essential for the regulation of vitamin C metabolism and distribution in rat hepatocytes, a cell type capable of synthesizing vitamin C, and in rat hepatoma cells that express the transporters involved.

glutathione depletion affects vitamin C metabolism and transport in rat cells capable of synthesizing vitamin C, but not in human cells unable to synthesize vitamin C, suggesting that the role of glutathione in vitamin C metabolism may depend on the cell type.

glutathione depletion by BSO treatment in rat cells that can synthesize ascorbic acid results in a blockade of vitamin C uptake by the plasma membrane, an effect that is reversible by glutathione repleting agents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the expression and function of SVCT1 and/or SVCT2 in hepatocytes is controlled by glutathione.
glutathione is an essential factor for controlling vitamin C metabolism and distribution in cells that are capable of ascorbic synthesis.
in the rat, but not in the human, glutathione plays a key role in the regulation of vitamin C transporters, and that in the rat glutathione depletion may lead to a vitamin C deficiency.
The main takeaway from our work is that

intracellular redox status, and in particular, the level of reduced glutathione, plays a crucial role in the regulation of the vitamin C transport machinery in rat hepatocytes, and rat hepatoma cell lines.
glutathione depletion is a useful tool to investigate the role of vitamin C transporters in cell physiology and disease.
glutathione plays a role in regulating vitamin C homeostasis by controlling vitamin C transporter expression and function, an effect that is cell specific and species dependent.
